verdicts.why: B passes all 10 checks, but its fidelity score falls to 0.787, below even the raw input's 0.841. Its processing explains the drop: two aggressive afftdn passes (nr=30, one with nf=-35), a 10 kHz lowpass, a hard gate (range 0.03) with pink noise mixed back in, and true peak sits right at the -1.0 dBTP limit. That is the underwater, processed sound the brief warned against. A's gentler chain improves fidelity to 0.868, removes the hum more fully (0.7 vs 3.1 dB) and leaves true-peak headroom at -1.4. Its only weakness is that the quiet passages are evened less (dip gap -4.4 vs -2.4 dB, failing that check), though they are still clearly lifted from -8.4.

A passes all 10 checks, but its fidelity falls to 0.787, below the raw input's 0.841. That fits its heavy chain: two afftdn passes at nr=30, a 10 kHz low-pass, ten notch filters, a gate and added pink noise, which is the 'underwater' sound the client asked to avoid. B's lighter chain beats the input at 0.868, removes the hum more fully (0.7 vs 3.1 dB) and has more true-peak headroom. B does fail levels_evened: the quiet passages were lifted from -8.4 to -4.4 dB, not as far as A's -2.4, and its gate threshold is hard-coded. That is a real gap, but less serious than A's loss of natural sound.

B sets the music level from measured loudness of the voice and the bed, so it adapts to the inputs. A uses a hard-coded -20 dB cut, which only fits this one file. B also ducks from the voice's actual speech segments with smooth ramps that bring the music back in pauses of 0.6 s or more, giving a much deeper duck (21.1 vs 9.4 dB), a larger voice-to-music margin (22.5 vs 17.2 dB) and higher voice fidelity, all of which serve the 'words easy to understand' requirement. A's gentle 6:1 sidechain compressor only gets about 9 dB of ducking. Both scripts hit loudness, true peak and the tail cleanly, so ducking quality and robustness are what decide it.

A ducks the music by 21 dB and keeps the voice 22.5 dB above the bed, against B's 9.4 dB duck and 17.2 dB margin, so A's words come through more clearly. A also scores higher on voice fidelity (0.961 vs 0.943). A's method is sturdier too: it sets the music level from the measured loudness of both files and builds a ducking curve from the speech timing that starts lowering the music before each sentence. B uses a fixed -20 dB cut on the music that only suits this one file, and its compressor reacts to the voice, so the first syllables can poke through. A's one weakness is that its fade-out begins right at the last word, which shortens the swell, but B's shallower duck matters more for a brief that says the words must stay easy to understand.

A's sidechain duck only pulls the bed down 5.5 dB. That leaves the voice 3.5 dB below the music, so the voice_above_music, ducks and voice_intact checks all fail and the copy gets buried, which is a non-starter on AM. B trims each line's silence, sets the bed level from measured loudness, and draws an explicit 16 dB duck envelope that comes back up between lines; the result is a 22.8 dB voice-over-music margin, 0.933 voice fidelity and 13/13 checks passed. B also fades the bed and sting out properly, ending at -59.7 dB against A's -31.1 dB. Its scripting is denser, but it's parameterized and holds up better.

B fails three checks that matter. Its music bed stays louder than the voice (-3.5 dB voice-to-music), it ducks only 5.5 dB, and voice fidelity is just 0.588, so the voice comes out buried and squashed. That happens because it runs the bed at a fixed 0.7 gain into a gentle sidechain compressor and never matches levels between voice and music. A trims silence from each line, sets the music level relative to the measured voice loudness, and uses a planned 16 dB duck that comes back up between lines. It passes all 13 checks and ends cleanly at -59.7 dB, while B relies on a 0.1 s fade that leaves -31 dB at the end.
